label: *Franks* Violation — False Statement or Material Omission in Affidavit
motion_heading: The Warrant Affidavit Contained Material Falsehoods or Omissions

review_conditions.display_note: The affiant's intent is unknown. This section was drafted anyway, but a *Franks* hearing requires a substantial preliminary showing that the false statement or omission was deliberate or made with reckless disregard for the truth; negligence or innocent mistake isn't enough. Develop evidence of intent before filing, or cut this section.
The affiant may not have known what other officers knew. Check when other officers' knowledge can support a *Franks* challenge.
Expect the prosecution to call this an innocent mistake. Lead with the facts showing the affiant knew, or should have known, the truth.

*Franks* also requires that the corrected affidavit fail to establish probable cause. Before filing, rewrite the affidavit without the false statement, and with any omitted facts added, and check whether what's left still supports the warrant.

excluded_explanations.display_note: The false statement or omission looks like a clerical error. *Franks* requires deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard for the truth, not a mistake. If discovery shows more, this issue may become viable.

sentences.text: A defendant is entitled to an evidentiary hearing on the validity of a search warrant affidavit upon a substantial preliminary showing that the affiant knowingly and intentionally, or with reckless disregard for the truth, included a false statement in the affidavit that was necessary to the finding of probable cause.

If, after excising the false material or including the omitted information, the affidavit's remaining content is insufficient to establish probable cause, the warrant must be voided and the fruits of the search excluded.
The same analysis applies to material omissions from the affidavit, not just affirmative false statements.

practice_notes: A *Franks* hearing requires more than pointing to an error — the defense must make a substantial preliminary showing of deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard, not mere negligence.
Consider pairing this with a good-faith exception rebuttal (*Leon*), since a *Franks* violation is one of the recognized exceptions to good-faith reliance on a warrant.
_author_notes: omissions_extension has no authority yet, so it never renders. Franks itself addresses false statements; the omissions extension is circuit-level doctrine. A possible 9th Circuit source is United States v. Stanert, 762 F.2d 775 (9th Cir. 1985) — unverified. Alaska authority not yet researched.
The franks_intent_unknown review note states the Franks intent standard from general knowledge; it hasn't been checked against the opinion. Unverified.

2026-10-12: warrants are no longer an encounter event. The trigger is a search with a search warrant (q_search_justification), or an arrest on an arrest warrant (q_arrest_warrant); each warrant question is reached only after its event.

REVIEW CAREFULLY (2026-10-13, the maintainer chose option A): q_intent (deliberate / reckless / negligent, a mental-state conclusion) was replaced by q_affiant_knowledge, a checklist of facts about what the affiant knew; anything but a clerical error alone includes the issue, and clerical_error alone gives the franks_intent_insufficient near miss. q_materiality ('would the affidavit still establish probable cause?', the court's question, required 'no') was removed: materiality is now the franks_materiality review note, shown whenever the issue is included. q_affidavit_accuracy was reworded to drop 'material' (ids unchanged). The franks_other_officers, franks_mistake_argument, franks_materiality and reworded near-miss notes are Claude drafts. Claude doesn't know how the Ninth Circuit or Alaska treat other officers' knowledge, so that note tells the attorney to check.
